headline: MCP Inspector: A Complete Debugging Workflow for MCP Servers
description: A practical debugging loop for MCP servers with the MCP Inspector: the client-proxy-server architecture, the stderr rule, reading the inputSchema contract your agent actually sees, sandboxed local development, and what the 2026-07-28 stateless spec changes.

mainEntity.name: Why does my MCP server disconnect with JSON parse errors?

acceptedAnswer.text: Almost always console.log on a stdio server. stdout is the JSON-RPC channel, so any plain-text logging written there is injected into the message stream and breaks the parser. Use console.error instead, which the MCP Inspector renders in its server output pane. Dependencies matter too: a library that logs to stdout can poison the stream without any logging in your own code.

mainEntity.name: Why don't my code changes show up in the MCP Inspector?

acceptedAnswer.text: The Inspector proxy spawned your server as a child process when you connected, and rebuilding does not restart it. You must reconnect in the Inspector after every rebuild, or you are testing the previous build.

mainEntity.name: Can I see a tool's data types and validation rules in the MCP Inspector UI?

acceptedAnswer.text: Not currently. The tool form renders fields from inputSchema without surfacing data types or validation constraints, which is tracked as issue 1388 in the MCP Inspector repository. Until it lands, read the raw tools/list JSON through the Inspector's raw message view, or run the Inspector in CLI mode with --method tools/list piped through jq, which prints the contract exactly as an agent receives it.

mainEntity.name: Is the MCP Inspector safe to run?

acceptedAnswer.text: On a current version with its auth token intact, it is reasonable. Below version 0.14.1 it is not: CVE-2025-49596, rated CVSS 9.4, allowed remote code execution through an unauthenticated proxy and was exploitable via DNS rebinding from a web page. Stay current, never set DANGEROUSLY_OMIT_AUTH, leave the default localhost-only binding in place rather than setting HOST=0.0.0.0, and treat inspecting an untrusted server as running that server, ideally via the published container image.

mainEntity.name: Can I use the MCP Inspector in CI or a script?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, that is what the --cli flag is for. CLI mode drops the browser and prints JSON, so --method tools/list and --method tools/call --tool-name X --tool-arg key=value can be piped into jq and asserted in a shell script. It also works against remote servers with --transport http and --header for authentication. The repository positions this as the loop to use with AI coding assistants because the output is machine-readable.

mainEntity.name: Why does the MCP Inspector time out on a tool that works fine?

acceptedAnswer.text: Inspector timeouts are independent of your server's, and whichever fires first is the one you see. MCP_SERVER_REQUEST_TIMEOUT defaults to 300000 ms, but MCP_REQUEST_MAX_TOTAL_TIMEOUT defaults to 60000 ms and acts as the hard ceiling once progress notifications begin resetting the per-request clock. Raise both for long-running operations or anything involving elicitation, where a human is in the loop.

mainEntity.name: Does the MCP Inspector work with the 2026-07-28 stateless specification?

acceptedAnswer.text: The Inspector tracks the specification, so check its release notes against the revision you are targeting. In raw traffic the practical difference is that there is no initialize handshake and no Mcp-Session-Id header: requests are self-contained and carry protocol version, client info, and capabilities in _meta, with server/discover available for fetching capabilities up front.

mainEntity.name: Should I test MCP servers only through the MCP Inspector?

acceptedAnswer.text: No, but more of it can be automated than most people realize. UI mode is for interactive work such as exploring, diagnosing, and reading protocol traffic. CLI mode covers scripted checks and CI. For unit-test-speed coverage, the official Python and TypeScript SDKs both support in-process clients, so a test suite can drive a server directly with no subprocess and no port.
